title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks; preregistration id cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) to evaluate whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration relative to plain single‑shot generation. Execution completed 600 episodes and used 301 model calls. Observed outcomes: baseline = 299/300 valid (99.667%); guarded = 300/300 valid (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered planning assumption used for power calculations (planned baseline pass rate = 0.40) was contradicted by the observed near‑ceiling baseline, removing statistical headroom for the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target. We report preregistered design choices, execution accounting, confirmatory statistics, a post‑hoc inferential sensitivity bound tied to the observed contingency counts, and artifact‑grounded recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations. All run artifacts and analysis outputs are archived in the execution manifest referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction:
Translating operator intent to device configuration is a core NetOps task. Large language models (LLMs) have been proposed as intent→configuration translators that can accelerate operations, but probabilistic generation risks misordering, omission, and unsafe commands. Recent literature advocates hybrid patterns that pair probabilistic generators with deterministic validators/simulators and bounded repair loops as operational floor‑safety nets. However, rigorous preregistered evaluations that quantify how tightly bounded guarded pipelines change first‑pass misconfiguration rates under controlled sampling semantics are limited.

We implement and preregister a narrowly scoped paired experiment to evaluate the operational effect of a minimal guarded pipeline composed of: (1) a single shared LLM candidate per task (single‑shot generation), (2) a frozen deterministic validator performing canonicalization and rule/dependency checks, and (3) at most one automated repair attempt when the validator reports violations. The core research question is: Can this minimal guarded pipeline reduce first‑pass misconfiguration rate relative to plain single‑shot generation under a controlled paired design? Our contributions are (i) a preregistered paired experiment with deterministic seed generation and archived per‑task artifacts, (ii) confirmatory statistics derived from those artifacts, (iii) a compact post‑hoc sensitivity quantification tied to the observed contingency counts, and (iv) artifact‑grounded recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations.
sections.related_work: Work applying LLMs to network configuration and intent translation has grown rapidly. Recent system demonstrations show promising intent→configuration synthesis in lab settings but also document failure modes—misordering, omission, and overconfidence—that affect operational safety [1]. Parallel work in adjacent domains (medical QA, code repair) shows that verifier‑assisted and retrieval‑augmented pipelines reduce factual errors and improve grounding, motivating similar guarded architectures for NetOps [2,3]. Classic deterministic network verification (header‑space analysis, specification‑based checking) provides algorithmic foundations for validators that can statically check reachability and policy constraints without live execution [4]. Survey and review articles emphasize the generate→verify→repair design pattern and highlight auditability and human‑oversight concerns as open challenges for production NetOps adopters [5]. Our study positions itself at the intersection of these strands by executing a preregistered paired evaluation that directly measures first‑pass validity under an explicit validator+repair floor‑guardrail.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and hypotheses: The experiment was preregistered (cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) and registered two confirmatory hypotheses: H1 — the guarded pipeline reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) versus single‑shot generation; H2 — one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations. The preregistration included the planning assumption baseline pass rate = 0.40 used for power computations; that assumption is reported here for transparent interpretation.

Design and sampling semantics: We used a paired within‑task design with a fixed deterministic seed list of 300 tasks produced by a frozen task generator. Each seed produced an intent and canonical reference configuration. The shared_initial_candidate semantics were preregistered: the same single LLM candidate per seed served as the baseline response and as the starting point for guarded validation and potential repair. Planned episodes = 600, initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1, maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1.

Model configuration and sampling determinism: The declared generation model was gpt-5-mini. Execution accounting records that the model configuration file is execution/model_configuration.json (sha256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). That artifact records "temperature": null. A null/unset temperature is not evidence of deterministic sampling (temperature=0); therefore sampling determinism was unspecified for the generation calls. This unspecified sampling determinism means generator variance could differ across runs and is a factor that can affect marginal success rates and discordant‑pair counts; the preregistered design did not force deterministic sampling.

Validator and repair semantics: The frozen deterministic validator canonicalized outputs to a normalized AST and applied static workflow and dependency checks encoded in the task payloads. Scoring used a full intent‑constraint rule: success required satisfying required_sequence, expected_final_state, and workflow policies. The repair adapter was invoked only when the validator reported violations, received structured violation codes plus the shared candidate, and was limited to one automated repair attempt per episode; repaired outputs were revalidated by the same validator. Contamination, exclusion, and replacement rules were preregistered and applied deterministically.

Primary estimand and analysis: The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistered primary test was the exact McNemar two‑sided test (α=0.05) with paired bootstrap percentile 95% CIs (10,000 resamples, seed specified). Missingness/retry policies and sensitivity treatments were preregistered; the primary analysis uses the 'complete_pair_primary' treatment documented in the preregistration. All per‑task artifacts, canonicalized responses, validator traces, repair prompts/responses, and analysis code were archived and are the authoritative source for reported counts.
sections.results:
Execution accounting (artifact‑derived): Planned episodes = 600; completed episodes = 600; complete pairs analyzed = 300. Model calls used = 301 (300 shared initial generations + 1 repair invocation). No provider or infrastructure failures occurred under the preregistered retry policy; no deterministic contamination exclusions were applied.

Primary outcomes (archived counts): Baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.667%); Guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). Paired contingency: n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00. Absolute paired difference = 1/300 ≈ 0.0033333. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Repair outcomes: the single allowed automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]).

Verified discordant episode: the single discordant pair is pair-000229 (task-000229). Archived raw-result records show the baseline episode scored 0 (VALIDATION_FAILED) on its single attempt and the guarded episode scored 1 (VALID_CONFIGURATION) after the guarded pipeline invoked the repair adapter (baseline attempt_count=1, guarded attempt_count=2; model_calls_used baseline=1, guarded=2). These exact per-episode values are present in the execution manifest and raw_results artifacts and are the source of the contingency counts.

Post‑hoc sensitivity bound: observed discordant total = 1, which constrains the maximum resolvable absolute paired difference to 1/300 ≈ 0.00333. The preregistered target corresponding to a ≥50% relative reduction from a planned baseline of 0.40 would have required on the order of 90 net discordant pairs favoring guarded outputs; that target is incompatible with the observed near‑ceiling baseline and explains why the preregistered large relative effect was not detectable.
sections.discussion:
The archived contingency (n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0) directly constrains inference: with a single discordant pair, McNemar inference lacks the discordant‑pair signal required to detect large preregistered relative reductions. This outcome derives from the observed near‑ceiling baseline and the shared_candidate pairing semantics, both preregistered and documented in the execution artifacts. Practical lessons: when the operational estimand is remediation of a single generated plan (shared candidate), power planning must account for expected baseline prevalence and the reduced expected discordance; conversely, independent‑draws designs address different operational claims and typically produce larger expected discordance for the same marginal probabilities.

Repair effectiveness here is conditional on initial failure; the run observed 1/1 repairs succeeded but the estimate is imprecise (95% CI wide). To estimate repair reliability precisely, future studies should ensure a planned number of initial failures—via calibrated task difficulty or adversarial augmentation—and preregister the conditional estimand and its targeted precision. Our frozen deterministic validator produced structured traces (normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes, repair_applied) that materially aided diagnosis of the single failure and the minimal edit the repair applied; maintaining such traces is essential for explainable NetOps guardrails. Finally, because validation here was static rather than runtime emulation, the reported success rates are conditional on the validator's static semantics; integrating emulation is necessary when runtime control‑plane or dataplane effects are material to operational claims.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=300 pairs) comparing single‑shot LLM generation (gpt-5-mini) to a guarded pipeline consisting of a frozen deterministic validator and a single automated repair iteration. Baseline single‑shot generation yielded 299/300 valid outputs and the guarded pipeline yielded 300/300 valid outputs. The single automated repair corrected the lone invalid baseline output, but the observed near‑ceiling baseline contradicted the preregistered planning assumption (baseline pass rate = 0.40) and removed statistical headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction. Future confirmatory NetOps evaluations should (a) calibrate task difficulty to produce sufficient initial failures or target discordant counts, (b) preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets explicitly, and (c) include emulation to measure runtime semantic effects when operational deployment claims are intended. All raw outputs, validator traces, repair traces, the execution manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived and enumerated in the Disclosure Statement to permit reproduction of the reported counts and intervals.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.
The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicts that assumption and removed headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction.
Sampling semantics (shared_initial_candidate) reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs available to McNemar inference.

Validation used deterministic configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; actual runtime consequences of configurations were not executed and remain unmeasured.

H2 repair‑success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
